paper.title: Immigrants' Effect on Native Workers: New Analysis on Longitudinal Data
paper.code_data_availability: No data availability statement appears in the article body. The dagger footnote on p. …

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: outcomes, treatment, controls, linkage and sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: the full population registers (used for the municipality immigrant shares and for the dispersal-policy settlement shares)
variables_mentioned: stock of employed immigrants by municipality

registers.name_in_paper: the O*NET database (US Bureau of Labor Statistics)
registers.role: task intensities (manual, communication, cognitive) of each occupation, used to build the complexity index

linkages: workers linked to establishments and to establishment industry and location via IDA
occupational task intensities linked from O*NET to Danish four-digit ISCO-88 occupation codes (the link to the Danish registers is described in the online Appendix)
individuals linked to their municipality of residence, and in the difference-in-differences design to their 1994 municipality
refugee-country immigrants linked to their municipality of first settlement 1986-1998 to build the shares s_cm used in the instrument

sample.universe: Individuals aged 18-65 in Denmark who were not attending school and not permanently disabled (the 'working-age population'), 1991-2008; outcome analysis restricted to Danish-born natives, split into low skilled (no college) and high skilled (college educated)
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year for Tables 6 and 7 and Figures 4-7; person (one long difference) for Table 8; municipality for Table 5
selection_rules: select individuals between 18 and 65 years old, not attending school and not permanently disabled
restrict the outcome analysis to a panel of Danish-born individuals
focus on those without college education (low skilled); high-skilled (college-educated) natives shown for comparison
panel regressions (equation 1): include all individuals employed in November of each year, 1995-2008
the occupational index and the hourly wage exist only for individuals employed at the end of November; the employment variable is measured for every native individual

difference-in-differences and cumulated regressions (equations 2 and 3): a strongly balanced panel of natives aged 21-51 in 1994, who stay in the sample continuously unless they become disabled, leave Denmark or die within 1991-2008
in the balanced panel, distinguish those employed as of November 1994 from those not employed in November 1994
difference-in-differences regressions include only individuals in the top-quartile and bottom-quartile municipalities of immigration exposure (the two intermediate quartiles are left out)
the empirical analysis uses a 20 percent random sample of native individuals; immigrant shares are calculated on the full population to avoid measurement error
geography: the 97 municipalities that can be identified consistently from 1988 to 2008, merging Frederiksberg with Copenhagen
sample.n_observations: 1,564,737 / 1,816,727 / 1,864,027 person-years in the low-skilled panel regressions (Table 6) and 2,860,183 / 3,125,934 / 3,160,757 in the high-skilled ones (Table 7); 71,053 individuals in the cumulated balanced panel (Table 8); 97 municipalities (Table 5)
sample.n_individuals: a 20 percent random sample of Danish native individuals; Figures 4-7 print no N

construction_notes: Complexity index = ln((Communication + Cognitive)/Manual), following Ottaviano, Peri, and Wright (2013); the skill content of each two-digit ISCO occupational grouping is the population-weighted average of the underlying four-digit ISCO occupations.

Hourly wage includes mandatory payments to pension schemes and is deflated by the Danish consumer price index; because pension data exist only from 1995, wages net of pension contributions are used whenever pre-1995 data are included (footnote 15).
Fraction of year worked equals one for a full-time employee throughout the year and a fractional value equal to the share of the regular working year spent at work otherwise.
Occupational mobility equals one whenever the individual changes four-digit ISCO-88 occupation between t-1 and t.

Treatment S_mt = F_mt/P_mt uses employment counts; the instrument Shat_mt = (sum_c s_cm x F_ct)/P_m1988 uses working-age population, which the authors describe as a further degree of exogeneity (footnote 28).

The eight refugee countries are Yugoslavia, Somalia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Iran and Lebanon; Bosnia is included in the actual inflow but excluded from the instrument because a special Bosnia Programme may have reduced the randomness of location (footnote 27).
s_cm is country c's share of new refugee immigrants whose first location was municipality m between 1986 and 1998, so that sum_m s_cm = 1 (footnote 26).

Immigration exposure for the difference-in-differences design is the population-weighted distribution of the 1994-2008 difference in the predicted refugee-country immigrant share; treated = top quartile, control = bottom quartile (footnote 22).

Event time: 1994 is year 0, years 1 to 14 are the treatment period, years -3 to 0 the pretreatment period; the year-0 interaction is omitted because municipality and year effects are included (footnote 23).

Occupation categories used in the occupation-by-year effects are unskilled worker (reference), skilled worker, intermediate professional, higher grade professional and manager; regions are the five Danish administrative regions and industries the eight one-digit NACE industries (footnote 24).
Table 8 cumulated outcomes use 46 weeks as the usual full-time work-year for a Danish worker (footnote 34), and the present discounted value of earnings uses a 4 percent annual discount rate.

Young/old and low/high tenure splits: the text on p. 27 defines young as aged 21-46 in 1994 and old as 47-61, while the notes to Figure 6 (p. 28) define young (old) as aged 21-36 (37-51); low (high) tenure is less than (at least) 4.35 years in the 1994 establishment, the sample-average tenure.

Extraction scope: every printed regression coefficient in Tables 5, 6, 7 and 8 is recorded as one claim (5 + 42 + 42 + 40 = 129), together with 23 claims read from the results figures (Figures 4-7, including one pre-trend test). Figures 1, 2 and 3 are descriptive and carry no tested claim. The online Appendix (Tables A.1-A.2, Figure A.1) is not part of this PDF and its numbers are not recorded.

claims.statement: An increase in the refugee-country immigrant share of municipal employment did not significantly change the occupational complexity of employed low-skilled natives, identified within worker-establishment spells (OLS estimate, Table 6, column (1)).

treatment.label: refugee-country immigrant share of employment in the municipality (S_mt)

register_source.value: IDA (Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research) for employment counts; the immigrant shares of each municipality are calculated on the full Danish population registers rather than on the 20 percent sample, to avoid measurement error

definition.value: S_mt = F_mt/P_mt, where F_mt is the stock of employed immigrants from the eight refugee countries (Yugoslavia, Somalia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Iran, Lebanon) and P_mt is total employment in municipality m in year t; the coefficient captures the effect on the outcome of an increase in refugee-country immigrants by 1 percentage point of employment

timing.value: contemporaneous: the municipality-by-year share in the same year as the outcome, annually 1995-2008

register_source.value: IDA (Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research): annual occupation of each employed individual (four-digit ISCO-88), linked to task intensities from the O*NET database of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (link to the Danish registers described in the online Appendix)

definition.value: Index of the complexity of the tasks performed on the job. Task intensities (manual, communication, cognitive) of each occupation come from the O*NET database (US Bureau of Labor Statistics) and are aggregated following Ottaviano, Peri, and Wright (2013); complexity = ln((Communication + Cognitive)/Manual), increasing in communication and cognitive content and decreasing in manual content. Measured only for individuals employed at the end of November.

timing.value: measured in November of each year t, 1995-2008, contemporaneously with the municipal immigrant share

units.value: log points of occupational complexity per one-unit change in the refugee-country immigrant share of employment; equivalently the printed coefficient read as a percent change in occupational complexity per 1 percentage point increase in the share

estimand.target_population: employed low-skilled Danish-born natives of working age in Danish municipalities, 1995-2008
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous (same-year) effect, estimated on the annual panel 1995-2008

population.description: Employed low-skilled (no postsecondary education at panel entry) Danish-born natives natives aged 18-65, not attending school and not permanently disabled, employed in November of each year between 1995 and 2008; the analysis uses a 20 percent random sample of native individuals
subgroups_defined: low skilled (no postsecondary education) vs high skilled (college educated)
population.selection: Danish-born individuals of working age, employed in November of each year (occupational index and hourly wage exist only for those employed at end-November); skill group fixed by education at panel entry; 20 percent random sample of natives, with immigrant shares computed on the full population registers

identification.source_of_variation: the Danish refugee dispersal policy in place between 1986 and 1998, which distributed all incoming refugees across municipalities on the basis of nationality and family size only, combined with the 1995-2003 surge of inflows from eight refugee countries that followed the enclaves created by that policy

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the individual-by-unit fixed effects, industry-by-year and region-by-year effects and the individual controls, the municipal refugee-country immigrant share is uncorrelated with the remaining determinants of the native outcome
key_assumptions.supported_by: the extensive fixed effects are argued to absorb any heterogeneity in employee-establishment matches, 'reducing drastically the scope for omitted variable bias'; the paper also argues that because refugee locations were centrally decided the OLS estimates may not be upward biased

lhs: refugee-country immigrant share of employment in the municipality
rhs: unobserved determinants of municipal labor demand

implies_edges.from: unobserved determinants of municipal labor demand
implies_edges.to: refugee-country immigrant share of employment in the municipality

key_assumptions.assumption: Immigration in the municipality of residence is a good proxy for the intensity of a native worker's exposure to the competition and the opportunity brought by those immigrants
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper notes that only around 10 percent of workers who move across establishments each year change municipality, so municipalities are rather self-contained labor markets

threats_discussed: immigrants responding to labor demand by moving to growing regions (the usual upward bias in area studies)
persistent pre-1994 trends in native outcomes correlated with the instrument (tested in Table 5)
attenuation bias from measurement error in immigrant shares (Aydemir and Borjas 2011), argued away because shares are computed on the full population registers
the worker-establishment fixed effects may miss important effects that are systematically different when workers change establishment
robustness_checks: OLS (columns 1, 3, 5) reported side by side with 2SLS (columns 2, 4, 6)
three alternative fixed-effect structures: worker-establishment spells, worker-municipality spells, and the whole individual experience
Table 5 pre-trend and EU-immigrant-share tests of the instrument
the same specifications run excluding Copenhagen (footnote 19; results stated to be very similar and not reported)
wages measured gross or net of mandatory pension contributions (footnote 15)

estimation.specification: equation (1) with individual-by-establishment fixed effects (Table 6, column (1))
estimation.clustering: municipality (initial municipality for individual fixed effects straddling several municipalities); heteroskedasticity-robust

heterogeneity.dimension: skill group of natives (low skilled vs high skilled)
heterogeneity.finding: Table 7 repeats these specifications for college-educated natives: the effects on complexity and manual tasks are much smaller (one half to one third of those for the less skilled), while the wage effects are larger for the high skilled

ambiguities: The printed coefficient is 0.255 (s.e. (0.326)) and carries no significance star; `sign` is recorded as 'null' because the estimate is not distinguishable from zero at the levels the table reports, while the point estimate itself is positive.

The baseline mean recorded here comes from Table 4, whose 1,864,027 observations correspond to the column (5)-(6) sample; this column estimates on 1564737 observations, for which no separate mean is printed.

evidence.how: Table 6 prints coefficients, standard errors in parentheses and significance stars only; no p-values and no confidence intervals are printed. Table significance legend as printed: *** significant at the 0.01 percent level, ** at the 1 percent level, * at the 5 percent level.

Table 4 (p. 12) reports this mean and standard deviation for the 1,864,027 employed low-skilled native person-years of the fixed-effect sample. It is a full-sample mean, not a control-group mean: the regressor is continuous and there is no control group. Table 4's N matches columns (5) and (6); columns (1)-(4) use somewhat smaller samples (1,564,737 and 1,816,727).

The refugee-country immigrant share enters the regression as a fraction, so the printed coefficient is the effect of a one-unit (100 percentage point) change in the share; multiplying it by 0.01 gives the effect of a 1 percentage point increase. For the two log outcomes that makes the printed number numerically equal to a percent change: the text reads 1.340 and 3.170 in the complexity rows as 1.3 and 3.1 percent, and 1.601 and 1.802 in the wage rows as 1.6 and 1.8 percent.

ambiguities: The printed coefficient is 0.151 (s.e. (0.129)) and carries no significance star; `sign` is recorded as 'null' because the estimate is not distinguishable from zero at the levels the table reports, while the point estimate itself is positive.

The baseline mean recorded here comes from Table 4, whose 1,864,027 observations correspond to the column (5)-(6) sample; this column estimates on 1564737 observations, for which no separate mean is printed.

evidence.how: Table 6 prints coefficients, standard errors in parentheses and significance stars only; no p-values and no confidence intervals are printed. Table significance legend as printed: *** significant at the 0.01 percent level, ** at the 1 percent level, * at the 5 percent level.

Table 4 (p. 12) reports this mean and standard deviation for the 1,864,027 employed low-skilled native person-years of the fixed-effect sample. It is a full-sample mean, not a control-group mean: the regressor is continuous and there is no control group. Table 4's N matches columns (5) and (6); columns (1)-(4) use somewhat smaller samples (1,564,737 and 1,816,727).

The refugee-country immigrant share enters the regression as a fraction, so the printed coefficient is the effect of a one-unit (100 percentage point) change in the share; multiplying it by 0.01 gives the effect of a 1 percentage point increase. For the two log outcomes that makes the printed number numerically equal to a percent change: the text reads 1.340 and 3.170 in the complexity rows as 1.3 and 3.1 percent, and 1.601 and 1.802 in the wage rows as 1.6 and 1.8 percent.

claims.statement: Low-skilled Danish natives who in 1994 lived in a municipality highly exposed to refugee-country immigration experienced a decline in fraction of year worked relative to those in low-exposure municipalities, over event years -3 to 14 around 1994 (cohort specification; Figure 7, Panel F. High tenure, fraction of year worked).

treatment.label: immigration exposure dummy M_m interacted with year dummies

register_source.value: constructed from the full Danish population registers: the population-weighted distribution of the 1994-2008 difference in the predicted refugee-country immigrant share across municipalities

definition.value: M_m equals 1 if the individual is in a municipality in the top quartile of the 1994-2008 difference in the predicted refugee-country immigrant share ('treated') and 0 if in the bottom quartile ('control'); the two intermediate quartiles are dropped. M_m is interacted with year dummies D(year = s) for s = -3..-1 and s = 1..14, with year 0 (1994) omitted

timing.value: exposure assigned by the 1994 municipality of residence (cohort) or by the municipality of residence in year t (area); pretreatment years 1991-1994, treatment period 1995-2008

definition.value: Fraction of the year worked: one for a full-time employee throughout the year, a fractional value equal to the share of the regular working year spent at work otherwise; measured for every native individual whether employed or not

timing.value: annually, event years -3 to 14 relative to 1994 (calendar 1991-2008)

units.value: difference in the fraction of the year worked between treated and control (vertical axis from -0.04 to 0.06 in Figures 4, 6 and 7 and -0.2 to 0.2 in Figure 5)

estimand.target_population: low-skilled Danish natives of working age who were employed in November 1994, at least 4.35 years of 1994 establishment tenure and who in 1994 resided in a municipality in the top quartile of predicted refugee-country immigrant exposure
estimand.time_horizon: year-by-year treatment-control differences for event years -3 to 14 relative to 1994 (calendar 1991-2008), with this claim about event years 12 to 15

population.description: Strongly balanced individual panel 1991-2008 of low-skilled (no college) Danish natives aged 21-51 in 1994 who were employed in November 1994, at least 4.35 years of 1994 establishment tenure, restricted to municipalities in the top and bottom quartile of immigration exposure
subgroups_defined: employed vs not employed in November 1994
young vs old in 1994
low vs high 1994 establishment tenure (4.35 years)
cohort (1994 location) vs area (year-t location) specification
population.selection: only individuals in top-quartile and bottom-quartile exposure municipalities are included; individuals are followed without further restrictions as they move into and out of employment and across jobs, leaving the panel only on disability, emigration or death

identification.source_of_variation: differential exposure of less educated natives to refugee-country immigrants based on their 1994 municipality of residence, with exposure quartiles defined by the refugee-country immigrant share predicted from the 1986-1998 dispersal policy, and a treatment period starting in 1995 when refugee-country immigration jumped discontinuously

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the post-1994 refugee inflow, outcomes of low-skilled natives in top-quartile and bottom-quartile exposure municipalities would have evolved in parallel after 1994, as they did over 1991-1994
key_assumptions.supported_by: the pre-treatment coefficients for event years -3 to -1 are plotted in every panel and the paper states that the pre-1994 treatment-control difference for all outcomes except one is not significantly different from zero

key_assumptions.assumption: Assignment of exposure is exogenous: the quartiles of predicted refugee-country immigrant exposure come from the dispersal policy, which allocated refugees independently of local labor demand
key_assumptions.supported_by: institutional description of the dispersal policy and the Table 5 tests (no correlation with pre-1994 outcome trends or with the EU immigrant inflow)

implies_edges.from: unobserved determinants of municipal labor demand
implies_edges.to: residence in 1994 in a municipality in the top quartile of predicted refugee-country immigrant exposure

key_assumptions.assumption: 1995 is the right break: the treatment period begins in 1995 because Figures 1 and 2 show a discontinuous increase in refugee-country immigration in that year, and year 0 (1994) is the omitted reference year
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figures 1 and 2 and footnote 23

threats_discussed: a pre-existing differential trend between exposed and non-exposed municipalities (checked over event years -3 to 0)
selective native mobility across municipalities, which the cohort/area comparison is designed to detect
early retirement ('efterloen') eligibility of the oldest workers in the last years of the window

the same design run for natives not employed in 1994 (Figure 5)
splits by age (Figure 6) and by 1994 establishment tenure (Figure 7)

evidence.panel: Panel F. High tenure, fraction of year worked
evidence.annotation: Low (high) tenure are those with less than (at least) 4.35 years in the firm in 1994.

evidence.how: Figure 7 plots the year-by-year coefficients and their 95 percent confidence limits against an axis running from -0.04 to 0.06 (-0.2 to 0.2 in Figure 5) but prints no numerical values; the paper states that Table A.1 of the online Appendix reports the estimates and standard errors for selected years, and the online Appendix is not part of this PDF.

No baseline level is printed for the difference-in-differences sample. Table 4 (p. 12) gives means for the employed low-skilled annual panel (occupational complexity 0.14, ln hourly wage rate 5.02, fraction of year worked 0.92) and footnote 17 (p. 11) states that the balanced panel used here has similar summary statistics, but no mean for this sample and outcome is printed.

Figures 4-7 print no number of observations and no number of individuals for the balanced panel; only Table 8, built on the same balanced panel of workers employed in 1994, reports N (71,053 overall).
